newsitem.title: USA: Museum of news hopes to revive faith in journalism.
newsitem.headline: Museum of news hopes to revive faith in journalism.

text.p: Here is the news. All of it.
We have news on a clay tablet, news by pigeon, news on a sound wave and a screen, good news, bad news, old and fresh.

As befits a superpower capital that generates more news than any other spot on the globe, Washington is becoming home to what its founders say is the first museum devoted exclusively to the what, where, when and why of news.

The Newseum, opening on Friday just across the Potomac River from downtown Washington in Rosslyn, Virginia, is a $50 million project of the Freedom Forum foundation, which fosters speech and a free press.

It opens at a time when the credibility of journalists in the United States is at a low, a time when the Internet and broadcast services are revolutionising the way people get information and clouding the definition of what makes news.

The Newseum aims at repairing that credibility by showing visitors how journalists actually work, giving people an inside look into the way editorial decisions are made and the pressures on the media to report and thrive economically.
The Newseum also aims at a loftier goal of showing, in the words of Allen Neuharth, the Freedom Forum chairman, "why a free press is essential to democracy."

"The reputation of journalism has never been lower," said Neuharth, the founder of USA Today and former head of the Gannett newspaper empire. He referred to surveys showing people consider journalists too cynical, biased and negative.

One recent poll by the Times/Mirror Centre for the People and the Press showed only 11 percent of Americans would say they have a "great deal" of confidence in the press, down from 19 percent in 1987.

The Newseum chronicles the reporting of major events in history. It includes Egyptian tablets nearly 4,000 years old, a letter from Christopher Columbus reporting the discovery of the "New World" and a pencil belonging to a reporter who died with Gen. George Custer at the 1876 Battle of Little Bighorn.
It shows how newspapers reported wars, disasters, scientific breakthroughs and social upheaval in the 20th century, when a revolution in communications shrunk the world.

And it depicts the leap from the printed word to the TV screen as the most immediate medium for delivering news. A display quotes legendary newscaster Walter Cronkite as saying television "literally has brought the world home in a box".

Reflecting the organisers' editorial judgment, the five news events selected as the highlights of recent years are the explosion of the space shuttle Challenger, the fall of the Berlin wall, the Gulf War bombing of Baghdad, the Oklahoma City bombing and the murder trial of O.J. Simpson.
That is just the history. The other side of the Newseum will draw on cutting edge communications technology and speak to the present and the future.
A videoscreen about 40 yards (metres) long will flash breaking news from television stations around the United States and the world brought in by satellite.
Visitors can play at being news announcers and sports commentators, and, on touch-screen displays, test their responses to everyday ethical and news judgment choices facing reporters and editors.
"This is not a shrine (to news)," Charles Overby, the president of the Freedom Forum said. "We will give people an idea of the complexity of the journalism on a daily basis."

Prominent journalists will lead debates on where the news business is going, considering issues like whether a talk show host is a purveyor of news and the concentration of media ownership in big corporations with disparate interests.

Visitors might draw inspiration from a collection of newspaper mottos on display. The Daily Herald of Arlington Heights, Illinois tells its readers, for example: "Our aim: to fear God, tell the truth and make money."
